Synopsis

Microsoft handed out infected Windows 95 demonstration disks to some 160 developers after a London developers' meeting in February 1995. One recipient scanned his disk before use and found the Form boot-sector virus.

Story

In February 1995, after a developers' meeting in London, Microsoft handed out Windows 95 demonstration disks to some 160 developers, and those disks carried the Form boot-sector virus. The affected scope was pre-release distribution, not the later August retail launch. That keeps the record narrow: official Microsoft demonstration media carried a common boot virus into the Windows 95 program.

Form was a boot-sector virus, so the risk lived in the media and boot path rather than in a Windows executable. The infected disk could matter before the operating system being tested ever ran. In the floppy era, a clean-looking vendor disk could be both installer and carrier.

One of the 160 recipients took the precaution of running his disk against a virus scanner before use, found Form, and informed Microsoft, which then warned everyone concerned. Kaspersky's historical summary says testing was put off until clean disks were issued. Contemporary reporting on Windows 95 virus problems also described installer failures and replacement disks, but the clearest supply-chain fact here is the demonstration-media contamination.

The impact was contained, but the case is historically useful. It shows the same failure pattern as LANSpool and later physical-media incidents: malware entered trusted duplication or distribution, and authenticity of packaging did not imply cleanliness of the bytes.
